title: $768M in, almost nothing out
lede: Webvan raised about $393M privately and $375M at its IPO, then paid for HomeGrocer with more than a billion dollars of its own stock. Shareholders received nothing in the bankruptcy.

blocks.title: Who owned Webvan before the IPO
blocks.subtitle: Share of 296.8 million shares outstanding, Oct 20, 1999.
blocks.source: Prospectus, principal stockholders table[^1]. Directors and officers as a group held 60.5%, including the venture funds represented on the board.

blocks.title: Money raised, by source
blocks.subtitle: $ millions. The HomeGrocer stock was not cash.
blocks.source: Prospectus[^1] and 10-K[^3]. Private rounds are net of issuance costs; the IPO figure is gross. Reuters later put the total at “more than $800 million in venture capital and IPO proceeds”[^19].

blocks.title: Where $914.5M of cash went
blocks.subtitle: Cash that came in from 1998 through 2000, and where it stood on December 31, 2000, six months before the shutdown. From the cash-flow statement in the 2000 annual report.

from.label: cash in, 1998 to 2000: $382.9M of preferred stock and $402.6M from the IPO (both net of costs), $101.1M of cash that came with HomeGrocer, and $27.9M of loans, leases and other stock sales (sum derived)

to.label: Warehouses, vans and equipment
to.note: Purchases of property, equipment and leasehold improvements: $32.7M in 1998, $64.3M in 1999 and $259.8M in 2000 (sum derived).[^3]

to.label: Running the business
to.note: Net cash used in operating activities: $2.2M in 1998, $58.8M in 1999 and $263.1M in 2000 (sum derived).[^3]

to.label: Still in the bank
to.note: $40.3M of cash and $171.6M of marketable securities on December 31, 2000.[^3] By March 31, 2001 this was reported as $115M.[^15]

to.label: Everything else (derived remainder)
to.note: What is left after the three reported figures: repayments of loans and leases, deposits, loans to shareholders and small investments, less the $2.9M of cash on hand at the start of 1998. We did not itemise it.

blocks.source: Webvan 10-K for 2000, consolidated statements of cash flows and liquidity discussion[^3]. The total, the three-year sums and the remainder are derived. The 10-K counts 28,750,000 shares sold in the IPO for $431.3M gross and $402.6M net; the prospectus covers 25 million shares, or $375M[^1]. The $1.04B paid for HomeGrocer was stock, not cash, and is not in this figure.

blocks.title: Sales peaked at $81.8M a quarter, with a loss more than twice as large
blocks.subtitle: Net sales and net loss by quarter, in $ millions, from the first orders to the last full quarter reported.

points.title: the store opens
points.text: The Bay Area Webstore launches on June 2, 1999. The first quarter brings in $0.4M.[^1][^3]

points.title: the IPO
points.text: Webvan goes public at $15 in November 1999 with $13.3M of sales for the whole year.[^1][^3]

points.title: the merger
points.text: HomeGrocer joins on September 5, 2000. The quarterly loss roughly doubles, from $74.4M to $148.0M.[^3][^6]

points.title: the peak
points.text: $81.8M of sales in the first full quarter with HomeGrocer (derived), against a $173.1M loss (derived).[^3][^6]

points.title: the retreat
points.text: Dallas closes in February 2001 and sales slip to $77.2M. The loss reaches $217.0M, including $73.9M of restructuring charges.[^7]

blocks.source: Quarterly 10-Qs and 10-K405/10-K[^3][^4][^5][^6][^7]. Q4 1999 and Q4 2000 are derived by subtracting nine-month results from full-year totals. Q4 2000 and Q1 2001 include HomeGrocer.
